groups.text: Two threads each add one to their own counter, twenty-five million times.
The card thread only writes card.
The SEPA thread only writes sepa.
They share no data, so there is nothing to lock, and no race.
Yet in one run, this took one thousand two hundred twenty ms.
With the two fields padded apart, the same work took two hundred forty-seven.
The reason is in the hardware.
Your C P U never reads one long from memory.
It moves a whole cache line, sixty-four bytes on xeighty-six.
This object is thirty-two bytes.
After a twelve-byte header and a four-byte gap, card sits at offset sixteen, and sepa at twenty-four.
Both counters live on the same line.
Each core has its own Lone and Ltwo caches, small fast memories right next to it.
Core one runs the card thread, and core two runs the SEPA thread.
Both cores keep a copy of the line.
To write to a line, a core needs the only valid copy.
So when core one writes card, core two's copy is invalidated.
Core two's next write has to take the line back first.
Now core one's copy is the invalid one.
The line bounces between the cores on almost every write, and both threads slow down.
This is false sharing.
The program shares nothing.
The hardware shares a lot.
The fix is to keep at least sixty-four bytes between fields that different threads write.
Padding pushes sepa onto a line of its own.
Now each core keeps its own line.
Both threads write, and no line has to move.
On the course's shared four-vCPU VM, one run showed a clear gap in all three rounds.
But an earlier, more careful J M H experiment on the same VM could not show any effect.
If the two threads land on hyperthreads of one physical core, they share its Lone and Ltwo, so there is no line to bounce.
The mechanism is certain.
The size of the effect is not, so measure on the hardware you run on.
And every count still ends at exactly twenty-five million.
False sharing costs time, never correctness.
